newsitem.title: USA: US official says EU move on Cuba ill-considered.
newsitem.headline: US official says EU move on Cuba ill-considered.

text.p: A top U.S. trade official said on Thursday the European Union was taking the World Trade Organisation (WTO) into "dangerous waters" by challenging a U.S. law aimed at foreign investment in Cuba.

Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat said EU efforts to bring the issue before a WTO dispute settlement panel played into the hands of anti-trade protectionists in the United States and took the global trade body into foreign policy areas where it did not belong.
"We believe the effort the European Union made is ill-considered and takes the WTO into very dangerous and uncharted waters," Eizenstat told a news conference.

On Wednesday, the United States blocked an EU request for a WTO panel to rule on the law that seeks to discourage foreign investment in properties of U.S. citizens confiscated by Fidel Castro's government after it took power in 1959.

Eizenstat was appointed special envoy by President Bill Clinton to try to soothe U.S. trading partners angered by the law and to beef up international efforts to bring democracy to Cuba. He has travelled to several capitals to explain the U.S. position and said he planned to go to France, the Netherlands, Sweden and Denmark this month to continue his efforts.
European anger over the Cuba law and another U.S. law aimed at large foreign investments in Libya and Iran has not spilled over into other trade relations, Eizenstat said.

He cited a recent U.S.-EU agreement to move ahead with an international agreement to eliminate tariffs on computers, software and other information technologies. But he criticised Europe for failing to move forward with agreements to eliminate duplicative regulatory standards that he said raised the cost of companies doing business in each others markets.
The agreements, he said, covered about $40 billion of trade between Europe and the United States.
The move to harmonise standards was started by a group of U.S. and European corporate leaders anxious to lower the cost of doing business in international markets.

Eizenstat said Europe was holding up five agreements covering telephone and information technology equipment, electrical products, pleasure boats and veterinary biologics because of a dispute over pharmaceutical standards.

He said the European Union wanted to go further on testing and certification standards than the U.S. Food and Drug Administration was allowed under U.S. law. He said he hoped the European Union would decide to go ahead with the other agreements before the business leaders, the so-called Trans-Atlantic Business Dialogue, meet in Chicago in November.
